opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely useful project, though I'd separate a few different ways it could have an impact, because they vary a lot in how much I'd expect from them.

The most straightforward one is transparency. A lot of what labs say about safety lives scattered across blog posts, system cards, policy documents, and occasional tweets. Just collecting it in one place and comparing companies on the same dimensions makes it much easier for journalists, policymakers, and employees to see what's actually been committed to and what hasn't. That's valuable even if nobody at the labs ever reads it, because it lowers the cost for everyone else to hold them accountable.

The second channel is something like competitive pressure. If there's a scorecard and your company is near the bottom, people inside notice, and that can give internal safety advocates a bit more leverage. I'd be cautious about overstating this, though. The pressure works best when the criteria line up with things that actually matter for safety. If the rubric rewards things that are easy to show externally, like publishing a policy document, you can get a bit of Goodharting, where companies optimise for the checklist rather than for substance.

And that's my main reservation. From the outside, it's really hard to evaluate the things I think matter most: How good are the dangerous capability evaluations in practice? How seriously does leadership take a bad result? What happens when a safety concern conflicts with a launch timeline? Those are mostly invisible to an external evaluator, so any outside rating will lean on proxies. I don't think that's a fatal flaw, since proxies are better than nothing, but I'd want readers to treat the scores as a rough signal rather than a precise ranking.

So overall I'd say it's positive and worth doing, mainly as an accountability and information tool. I just wouldn't expect it alone to move practices dramatically. It's most useful as one input alongside things like regulation, third-party audits, and people inside the companies pushing for better practices.

r001.rationale: The response describes scorecard-driven competitive pressure as a possible source of leverage for internal safety advocates, but it does not say that companies may improve safety when they regard AI Lab Watch’s ratings as legitimate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think AI Lab Watch is a genuinely useful thing to exist, though I'd want to be careful about how much I expect it to move the needle on its own.

The basic mechanism it's relying on is reputational pressure. You take a bunch of practices you think labs should be doing — things like having a responsible scaling policy, doing dangerous capability evaluations, having good security, publishing safety research, having internal governance that can actually say no — and you grade each company against them in a public, legible way. The hope is that nobody wants to be the one at the bottom of the list, and so over time the laggards catch up, and maybe the leaders get pushed to go a bit further so they can keep their position.

I think that mechanism does work to some extent. Companies care about how they're perceived, especially by the sort of people who read these things — potential hires, policymakers, journalists, safety researchers deciding where to work. When a company is visibly worse than its competitors on something concrete, that's a real cost, and it's much easier to get something changed internally when you can point at an external scorecard and say, "Look, we're getting dinged for this."

The main limitations I'd point to are a few things. First, the people doing the grading have limited visibility. A lot of what matters happens inside the labs and isn't public, so you end up grading what's observable — published policies, published research, public commitments — and that can bias you toward rewarding companies that are good at communicating rather than companies that are good at actually doing the work. Those are correlated, but they're not the same thing.

Second, there's the usual Goodhart problem. Once there's a checklist, it's tempting to optimize for the checklist. You can write a very nice-looking responsible scaling policy that doesn't actually constrain you very much. So the value of the thing depends a lot on how thoughtfully the criteria are designed and how willing the evaluator is to say, "You technically did the thing, but it doesn't count."

Third, I think reputational pressure mostly works on the margin. It's good at nudging companies to adopt practices that are relatively cheap and that their competitors already do. It's much weaker at getting a company to do something expensive that's genuinely against its competitive interest — delaying a launch, say, or not building something. For that you probably need regulation, or very strong internal culture, or both.

So my overall view is: it's a positive contribution, it raises the floor, it makes the conversation more concrete, and it gives people inside labs something to point to. I'd be surprised if it were the decisive factor in any big safety decision, but I don't think that's the right bar. If it makes a handful of practices slightly more standard across the industry, that's worth having. And I'd generally like to see more independent scrutiny of the labs, not less — including of the one I work at.

r001.rationale: The response says companies may respond to being ranked below competitors and leaders may try to keep their position. It does not communicate the condition that companies must regard AI Lab Watch’s scorecard as legitimate.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic theory of change is plausible: if you make it easier to see what AI companies are doing on safety, and where they’re falling short, that could create pressure for them to improve. But a lot depends on what you’re measuring and who pays attention to it.

The hard part is distinguishing practices that actually reduce risk from practices that are easy to observe. You don’t want a company to be able to improve its rating just by publishing more documents, without changing how it makes consequential decisions. And there’s a related difficulty that some safety work won’t be visible from outside, so you need to be careful about how you communicate uncertainty.

I’d be more optimistic if the assessments identified concrete, actionable improvements, and if people whose opinions matter to the companies used them. That could be employees, policymakers, or customers. Ultimately, I’d want to know whether a company changed a meaningful safety practice because of the scrutiny. That’s a much stronger signal of impact than whether the assessment got a lot of attention.

r001.rationale: The response says visible assessments could create pressure to improve, but it does not identify competition for higher ratings or make the incentive conditional on companies regarding the scorecard as legitimate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic theory of change is plausible: make it easier for outsiders to see what AI companies are doing on safety, and give companies a reputational incentive to improve. But a lot depends on what you measure and whether the people making decisions actually care about the assessment.

One concern is that the things you can assess from the outside are often things like whether a company has published a policy or made a commitment. Those can be useful, but they’re an imperfect proxy for whether the company will make good decisions when safety is costly. You don’t want to create an incentive to produce better documentation without improving the underlying practices.

So I’d be interested in evidence that the assessment is changing decisions inside companies. Are employees using it to argue for specific improvements? Are companies addressing substantive criticisms? That would make me more optimistic. I’d view it as a potentially useful source of external pressure, with quite a bit of uncertainty about how much it ultimately changes safety.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes reputational incentives and says impact depends on whether decision-makers care about the assessment, but it does not identify competition for higher ratings as the incentive.
